prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Imagine that Alice and Bob want to agree on a number that nobody else knows, but the only way they can talk is by shouting across a crowded square where everyone, including a woman named Eve who is determined to learn their secret, hears every word. It seems impossible, because anything Alice tells Bob, Eve hears as well, and yet a method for doing exactly this was published in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, and today it runs quietly every time your phone opens a secure connection to a website. The method depends on a kind of arithmetic in which one direction of travel is quick and the return journey is, for big enough numbers, so slow that no computer on Earth could finish it within the lifetime of the universe.

The arithmetic in question is the clock arithmetic you may have met at school, where you keep only the remainder after dividing by some fixed number. On an ordinary clock the fixed number is twelve, so that five hours after ten o'clock it is three o'clock, because fifteen leaves a remainder of three when divided by twelve. Alice and Bob will use a clock with twenty-three positions instead, which mathematicians call working modulo 23, and every calculation below ends with the instruction to divide by 23 and keep only what is left over. They also agree, openly and in front of Eve, on a base number, which we will take to be 5, and nothing about these two choices needs to be hidden.

What makes this clock useful is what happens when you raise the base to a power, meaning that you multiply 5 by itself that many times and then take the remainder. Five to the power of 2 is 25, which leaves 2 on the 23-hour clock, and five to the power of 3 is 125, which leaves 10, and if you carry on you get a sequence of remainders that bounces around the clock in an order that looks random, even though each step is perfectly predictable. Going forwards is easy, since given the power you simply multiply and reduce, and there are shortcuts such as squaring repeatedly so that even a power in the hundreds takes only a few steps. Going backwards is the hard direction, because if someone tells you that 5 raised to some unknown power leaves a remainder of 8 and asks which power it was, you have no better method than trying the powers one after another until one fits, and with a clock the size of the numbers used in real life that search never ends.

Now the exchange itself. Alice privately chooses a secret number, say 6, and Bob privately chooses his own, say 15, and neither of them tells anyone. Alice computes 5 to the power of 6, which is 15,625, and dividing by 23 leaves a remainder of 8, so she calls out the number 8 across the square. Bob computes 5 to the power of 15, which leaves a remainder of 19 on the same clock, and he calls out 19. Eve now knows the base 5, the clock size 23, and the two announced numbers 8 and 19, but she does not know the secrets 6 and 15 that produced them.

To finish, each of them takes the number they heard from the other and raises it to the power of their own secret. Alice takes Bob's 19 and raises it to the power of 6, which gives 47,045,881, and that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 23. Bob takes Alice's 8 and raises it to the power of 15, which is a number of fourteen digits, and that too leaves a remainder of 2, so both of them arrive at the number 2, which was never spoken aloud and which they can now use as a shared secret.

The reason they land on the same number is that raising a power to a power simply multiplies the exponents. Alice's announcement was 5 to the power of 6, and Bob raised that to the power of 15, giving 5 to the power of 6 times 15, which is 5 to the power of 90. Bob's announcement was 5 to the power of 15, and Alice raised that to the power of 6, giving 5 to the power of 15 times 6, which is the same 5 to the power of 90. Multiplication does not care about order, so the two routes meet at the same place, and taking remainders along the way does not disturb this because the remainder of a product depends only on the remainders of its parts. Each person could reach 5 to the power of 90 only because each held one of the two ingredients privately, and the ingredient each kept is exactly the one Eve is missing.

You might object that with a clock of only 23 positions Eve could simply try every power from 1 upwards until she found one that produces 8, and she could, which is why 23 is a toy. In real use the clock has hundreds of digits, or the same idea is carried out on a more exotic structure called an elliptic curve, which achieves similar strength with smaller numbers, and the secrets chosen are equally enormous, so that the list of possible powers is longer than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Nobody has proved that the backwards problem is impossible to shortcut, only that mathematicians have tried for decades without finding a fast method, and the whole arrangement stands on that long record of failure.

The name public-key cryptography comes from the fact that each person ends up holding a pair of linked numbers, one kept private and one that can be shown to the world, and the announced 8 and 19 above play the role of the public halves. Related schemes, of which the best known is called RSA after its inventors, use a different hard problem, the difficulty of splitting a huge number into its prime factors, to let anyone lock a message using a public number that only the owner of a matching private number can unlock. In everyday practice these slower methods are used only briefly at the start of a conversation to agree on a secret, after which both sides switch to a fast ordinary cipher that scrambles the real messages using the shared number as its key.

One weakness remains, which is that the exchange protects against someone who merely listens and does nothing against someone who can intercept and replace messages. If Eve could stand between the two and pretend to Bob that she was Alice, she would run one exchange with each of them and read everything passing through, so real systems add a second layer in which a public key is vouched for by a trusted authority whose signature can be checked, which is why your browser shows a padlock only when the site can prove who it is. The listening problem, however, which seemed unsolvable at the start, is settled by nothing more than remainders on a clock and the stubborn fact that running them backwards is far harder than running them forwards.
